picks.who: Gheranda Samhita · tr. S. C. Vasu, 1914
picks.quote: As by learning the alphabets one can, through practice, master all the sciences, so by thoroughly practising first the (physical) training, one acquires the Knowledge of the True.
picks.meaning: Learn the ABC, keep practising, and one day you can read anything. Practice first, and understanding follows.
picks.work: Gheranda Samhita, Chapter I, verse 5 (First Lesson), in The Sacred Books of the Hindus Vol. XV, The Yoga Sastra, Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914, p. 2 of the Gheranda section
picks.why: Slide 1 for beginners. Everyone remembers learning the alphabet, and letters turning into reading is exactly the theme: small pieces come together through practice. It is also a yoga text, it is public domain, and both checkers confirmed it word for word. I used the more literal meaning line the checker suggested.

picks.quote: The truth is, I had to work very hard... to make it look easy. I spent years whining... swearing… throwing my racket… before I learned to keep my cool.
picks.meaning: Federer won only 54% of the points in his 1,526 singles matches. Years of work and mistakes made it look easy.
picks.work: Roger Federer, 2024 Commencement Address, Dartmouth College, June 9, 2024 (official transcript on dartmouth.edu)
picks.why: The strongest real life and the easiest for anyone to relate to. The 54% number makes the point concrete: being good comes from years of doing, mistakes included. I added 'singles' to the meaning line because the card says the 1,526 matches were singles.

picks.quote: ...without consuming the juice of the divine nectar, how can we know the taste of the fruit? This is never possible.
picks.meaning: You can only know a mango's taste by eating it. Yoga is the same: you learn it by doing it.
picks.work: Yoga Makaranda (Yoga Saram), First Part, Ch. 1 Introduction, sec. 1.1 'Why should Yogabhyasa be done', p. 8; English translation by Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan (translators' note dated 15 Oct 2006) of the 1938 Tamil edition (Kannada edition 1934)
picks.why: The grandfather of the Ashtanga lineage, in his own printed words. You can't know a taste until you eat it, which is the theme as a picture. Checked word for word.

picks.who: Michael Faraday · Letter to Dr. Becker, 1860
picks.quote: I was never able to make a fact my own without seeing it... All the work had to be my own.
picks.meaning: In 1805 Faraday became a bookbinder's apprentice. He did simple chemistry experiments that cost a few pence a week.
picks.work: Letter to Dr. Becker, 25 October 1860, quoted in Silvanus P. Thompson, Michael Faraday, His Life and Work (1898), p. 244. The full letter is in Bence Jones, The Life and Letters of Faraday, vol. 2 (1870), pp. 439-440.
picks.why: A great scientist who started with no schooling, as a bookbinder's boy, and learned by doing things with his own hands. 'Make a fact my own' says it well. I split the meaning line into two short sentences. The facts are unchanged.

picks.quote: ...intellectual power and a knowledge of the scriptures alone do not lead to Self-realization... Practice alone is the path to atma labhah [gaining the Self].
picks.meaning: Reading and smart thinking are not enough. Jois began at 12, in 1927, and practiced daily long before he understood.
picks.work: Yoga Mala, Pranayama section. Written in Kannada from 1958, first published in India in 1962. English translation by Vishwanath Kadam and H. L. Chandrashekar, first published by Eddie Stern / Patanjali Yoga Shala in 1999, then by North Point Press in 2002. The linked scan is the 2010 North Point edition. Page number not confirmed.
picks.why: These are Jois's own words in his own book. That avoids the two famous lines that have no printed source ('99% practice' is only in Sharath's foreword, and 'all is coming' has none). The meaning line says he practised for years before he understood, which is the theme exactly.

picks.who: Auguste Rodin · Art (talks with Paul Gsell), 1912
picks.quote: ...no sudden inspiration can replace the long toil which is indispensable... to render the hand obedient to the commands of feeling.
picks.meaning: Paris's top art school said no to Rodin three times. He learned by working as a craftsman for about twenty years.
picks.work: Auguste Rodin, Art, conversations recorded by Paul Gsell, translated by Mrs. Romilly Fedden (Small, Maynard & Company, Boston, 1912), Chapter V 'Drawing and Color'
picks.why: Rejected three times, then twenty years of hands-on work, and then one of the greatest sculptors. 'Long toil' over 'sudden inspiration' fits the theme well. I made the meaning line simpler. The three rejections and the twenty years are in the card; the year 1857 was dropped to stay short.

picks.who: Wang Yangming · Instructions for Practical Life, 1518
picks.quote: The situation may be likened to a man traveling. When (by walking) he has covered a stage, he understands that stage... In this way he gradually reaches his destination.
picks.meaning: A traveller understands each part of the road only by walking it, and step by step he arrives.
picks.work: The Philosophy of Wang Yang-ming, trans. Frederick Goodrich Henke (Open Court, 1916), Book I, Instructions for Practical Life, Part II, p. 95. Public domain.
picks.why: This is the closest card to Boonchu's 'bits and pieces come together': you understand each stage only after you have walked it. It is a Chinese sage, which helps with the China audience, and it is public domain and checked word for word.

picks.who: Leonardo da Vinci · Notebooks, tr. Richter 1883
picks.quote: Wisdom is the daughter of experience.
picks.meaning: Leonardo started as a studio boy at about 14. By 1472, at age 20, he was a master painter.
picks.work: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, compiled and translated by Jean Paul Richter (first published London, 1883; Gutenberg text from the 1888 edition), Section XIX 'Philosophical Maxims. Morals. Polemics and Speculations', No. 1150. Italian original: 'La sapientia e figliola della sperientia'.
picks.why: Short and easy to screenshot. It is his own line, checked against the 1883 edition with the Italian beside it. He learned as a boy in a working studio. I split the meaning line into two sentences and kept the same facts.

picks.who: Shiva Samhita · tr. S. C. Vasu, 1914
picks.quote: I cannot describe the grandeur of this contemplation. He who practises, knows.
picks.meaning: Some things words cannot explain. Do the practice, and you will understand it yourself.
picks.work: The Siva Samhita, Chapter V, verse 166, in The Sacred Books of the Hindus Vol. XV, The Yoga Sastra, Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914, p. 80
picks.why: 'He who practises, knows' is the shortest version of today's theme in a yoga text. It works well near the end. Public domain, and checked word for word in two scans.

picks.quote: With every repetition you will discover some hitherto unnoticed defect... Obviate these defects, one by one, and in so doing you will come nearer and nearer to the spiritual essence...
picks.meaning: In 21 concerts, Hofmann played 255 different works from memory. He taught that each repeat shows one more thing to fix.
picks.work: Josef Hofmann, Piano Playing: A Little Book of Simple Suggestions (New York: McClure, 1908; first serialized 1907 by Curtis Publishing), chapter 'Playing "In Style"', p. 53 (scan: https://archive.org/details/pianoplayinglitt1908hofm). Same wording in the combined edition 'Piano Playing, with Piano Questions Answered' (Theodore Presser, 1920), which is the Project Gutenberg text.
picks.why: A good closing slide. Each time you repeat, you fix one more piece and come 'nearer and nearer', which is how practice feels from the inside. It ends the carousel on the theme of bits coming together.

backups: John Amos Comenius · The Great Didactic, 1657: 'Artisans do not detain their apprentices with theories ... they learn to forge by forging, to carve by carving, to paint by painting, and to dance by dancing.' Verified and public domain. The best swap for any sage.

Aristotle · Nicomachean Ethics II.1, 4th century BCE: 'For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre...' Fixed. The translation is public domain in the US only.
Saadi · Gulistan, 1258: 'However much thou art read in theory, if thou hast no practice thou art ignorant.' Verified, public domain.

Goethe · Wilhelm Meister's Journeyman Years, 1829: 'It is not enough to know, we must also apply; it is not enough to will, we must also do.' Verified. The alternate Maxim No. 2, 'Never by thinking, but by doing', is also checked.
John Dewey · Democracy and Education, 1916: 'An ounce of experience is better than a ton of theory...' Verified, public domain.

Shankara (attributed) · Vivekachudamani, 8th c. or later: 'A disease does not leave off if one simply utter the name of the medicine, without taking it...' Fixed. The authorship is doubted, so keep '(attributed)'.

Enrico Caruso · The Art of Singing, 1909: '...not by theory and reasoning, but simply oft repeated attempts.' Fixed. The best swap for any real life, but the wording is clunky and the text may have been put together from interviews.

Milarepa · Jetsun-Kahbum, c. 1488: '...went to sleep over my task, and so failed to put the doctrine to the test of practice.' Fixed. It reads like a real life even though it is labelled sage. Keep the sorcery and killings out of any caption.

Dogen · Bendowa, 1231: '...it is not actualized without practice, and it is not attained without realization.' Fixed. The English is a modern translation still under copyright, from the official Soto Zen site.

Xunzi · Works of Hsuntze (tr. Dubs), 1928: '...understanding it is not as good as doing it. ... He who carries it out, knows it thoroughly.' A strong fit, but held back because Xunzi was already used on 1 Oct. If it is ever used, take the card with the page-specific URL (page/n115) and confirm the 1 Oct line was a different passage.
pick.notes:
I picked a full set of 10: 5 sages on slides 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, and 5 real lives on slides 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Slide 1 is the Gheranda alphabet line, chosen for beginners. No quote words were changed. Four meaning lines were simplified with no new facts added. Gheranda uses the checker's more literal line. Federer adds 'singles', which the card supports. Faraday and Leonardo were split into two shorter sentences. Rodin was reworded and drops the year 1857. All meaning lines are 22 words or fewer, with no long dashes.

I left Xunzi out on purpose. There are 4 Xunzi cards, but all of them use the 1 Oct exception, and the repo has no record that the 1 Oct line was a different passage. The sages lean toward yoga and Asia, and the lives are all Western, so the carousel balances out.

Things to handle when posting:
(1) Krishnamacharya: the English is a 2006 translation still under copyright. Credit the translators, Lakshmi and Nandini Ranganathan.
(2) Federer: this is a modern speech, so keep the quote short and credit Dartmouth.
(3) Jois: the page number is not confirmed. Link only archive.org/details/yogamala0000jois, never archive.org/details/YogaMala, which is probably an unauthorized upload.
(4) Hofmann: the fact about 255 works in 21 concerts comes from Wikipedia citing Schonberg's The Great Pianists. The checker could not open the book itself.
(5) Faraday: leave out that Dr. Becker was Prince Albert's secretary, because of the royalty rule.
(6) Gheranda and Shiva Samhita both come from the same Vasu 1914 volume. The book spells it 'Siva Samhita'. I kept 'Shiva' because more readers will recognise it.
(7) Rodin: the translator is credited as Mrs. Romilly Fedden.

good.who: Gheranda Samhita · tr. S. C. Vasu, 1914
good.quote: As by learning the alphabets one can, through practice, master all the sciences, so by thoroughly practising first the (physical) training, one acquires the Knowledge of the True.
good.work: Gheranda Samhita, Chapter I, verse 5 (First Lesson), in The Sacred Books of the Hindus Vol. XV, The Yoga Sastra, Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914, p. 2 of the Gheranda section
good.meaning: You learn the ABC by using it, then you can read anything. Practice first, and understanding follows.
good.reason: I tried to refute this card and couldn't. (1) Wording: I downloaded the archive.org OCR (88861_djvu.txt) and verse 5 matches the quote word for word, including "(physical)" and "practising", in Lesson First right after verse 4 ("no strength like that which comes from discipline"). (2) URL: the hOCR page index puts the passage on leaf index 189, so page/n189 opens the right scan page. The next leaf is page 3 and the OCR shows a running head "2. THE GHERANDA SAMHITA", so p. 2 is correct. (3) Year: the Gheranda Samhita's own title page and the Vol. XV title page both say 1914 (Panini Office, Bhuvaneswari Asrama, Bahadurganj, Allahabad; printed at the Indian Press). The combined "Yoga Sastra" title page and the archive.org metadata say 1915. The second copy (archive.org/details/Gheranda_Samhita) says "First Published 1914-15" and has the same verse, with the OCR typo "piactising". So 1914 is correct for this section and the text is public domain. (4) Rules: the quote is 28 words. The meaning line is 17 words, plain English, no em dash. Gheranda is not on the used list (Svatmarama and Patanjali are different sources). There is no political, royal, disaster or religious-mockery content, and no inflated lineage claim. Optional, not required: a more literal meaning line would be "Learn the ABC, keep practising, and one day you can read anything. Practice first, and understanding follows."

good.who: Shiva Samhita · tr. S. C. Vasu, 1914
good.quote: I cannot describe the grandeur of this contemplation. He who practises, knows.
good.work: The Siva Samhita, Chapter V, verse 166, in The Sacred Books of the Hindus Vol. XV, The Yoga Sastra, Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914, p. 80
good.meaning: Some things words cannot explain. Do the practice, and you will understand it yourself.
good.reason: I tried to refute it and could not. I downloaded the OCR text of both archive.org scans. Scan india.history.resource.88861 (leaf 175, printed page 80; I confirmed this with the hOCR page index and page_numbers.json) reads: "166. I cannot describe the grandeur of this contemplation. He who practises, knows. He becomes respected by me." The second scan, sacredbooksofthehindusvol15sivasamhitawithsanskrittextscvasu1914_202002, has the same words on p. 80. The quote matches word for word. It stops at a full stop, so leaving out "He becomes respected by me" is honest and needs no ellipsis. The 1914 spelling "practises" is correct. Chapter V is right: its heading comes before this verse at p. 52, and the table of contents lists only Chapters I to V. The 1914 date is right too: both the Vol. XV title page and the Siva Samhita's own title page say "Printed by Apurva Krishna Bose at the Indian Press, 1914". The archive.org metadata says 1915, but only the Introduction to Yoga Philosophy section of that scan is dated 1915. The translator, Rai Bahadur Srisa Chandra Vasu, and the publisher, Panini Office, Bahadurganj, Allahabad, are both correct. The speaker is the god Siva talking to Parvati. The verses around it (162 to 168, on the Raja Yoga contemplation) say nothing about politics, war, crime or disasters, and the card does not mock any god. The Siva Samhita is not on this week's used list (Patanjali, Svatmarama and the Gita are separate works). It is 13 words long and in the public domain. The meaning line is 15 words, uses plain language and no em dash, and it is a text rather than a real life, so no fact is needed. It also fits the theme directly: you understand by doing, not by having it described to you. I also spot-checked the backup option in the notes, Ch. IV vv. 9-10 on p. 43 (leaf 138): "Through practice (abhyasa), success is obtained; through practice one gains liberation..." is in the scan as stated. V.166 is still the cleaner choice. Optional small change: the book spells it "Siva Samhita", so you could use that spelling in the who line to match the source.

good.quote: ...without consuming the juice of the divine nectar, how can we know the taste of the fruit? This is never possible.
good.work: Yoga Makaranda (Yoga Saram), First Part, Ch. 1 Introduction, sec. 1.1 'Why should Yogabhyasa be done', p. 8; English translation by Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan (translators' note dated 15 Oct 2006) of the 1938 Tamil edition (Kannada edition 1934)
good.meaning: You can only know a mango's taste by eating it. Yoga is the same: you learn it by doing it.
good.reason:
I downloaded the archive.org full text (https://archive.org/stream/YogaMakarandaKrishnamacharya/Yoga%20Makaranda%20Krishnamacharya_djvu.txt) and the quote is there word for word. The text reads: "...if we did not bother to taste its juice — without consuming the juice of the divine nectar, how can we know the taste of the fruit? This is never possible." The card starts the quote at "without" with an ellipsis, which is honest. It sits in sec. 1.1 under the running header "8 CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION", so it is on p. 8.

The title page confirms the other details: "Yoga Makaranda or Yoga Saram, First Part", "Written in Kannada", "Kannada Edition 1934", "Tamil Edition 1938". The translators' note is signed "Lakshmi Ranganathan, Nandini Ranganathan, October 15, 2006", and the preface is dated 10-10-1934. The context matches the meaning line: it is the mango-tree parable, ending "Without effort can anybody ever achieve anything? Similarly, even in the matter of yoga, unless it is practised with complete faith, no benefit will be gained." The meaning line is 19 words, plain, and has no long dash.

Rules check:
- The quote is about 21 words.
- Krishnamacharya is not on the used list.
- These are his own printed words in translation, so the lineage rule is met, and nothing inflates anyone's authorization.
- Nothing in the card touches politics, royalty, disaster or crime. The preface names the Mysore ruler, but that is not in the card.

Both the archive.org details page and the terebess PDF return HTTP 200. One caveat: the 2006 English translation is not public domain. A one-sentence quote with the translators credited is reasonable, but they should be named when it is posted. I changed only the work field: "Part 1" now reads "First Part", as on the title page, and I added the exact date of the translators' note.

good.quote: ...intellectual power and a knowledge of the scriptures alone do not lead to Self-realization... Practice alone is the path to atma labhah [gaining the Self].
good.work: Yoga Mala, Pranayama section. Written in Kannada from 1958, first published in India in 1962. English translation by Vishwanath Kadam and H. L. Chandrashekar, first published by Eddie Stern / Patanjali Yoga Shala in 1999, then by North Point Press in 2002. The linked scan is the 2010 North Point edition. Page number not confirmed.
good.meaning: Reading and smart thinking are not enough. Jois began at 12, in 1927, and practiced daily long before he understood.
good.reason:
I kept the quote but fixed several details.

What checks out:
- The quote matches word for word inside the linked item itself. Open Library's search-inside (which searches archive.org book text) finds it in yogamala0000jois (2010) and in two scans of the 2002 North Point edition: archive.org/details/yogamala0000jois_o5r6 and yogamala0000jois_h8s8. All three are borrow-only with a free account.
- The full text reads: "But intellectual power and a knowledge of the scriptures alone do not lead to Self-realization; the analysis of commentaries ... do not lead to Self-attainment. Indeed, it is not even enough to study Vedanta at length under the guidance of a Guru. Practice alone is the path to atma labhah [gaining the Self]." Both ellipses are honest, and the bracketed gloss is printed in the book.
- The passage sits under the PRANAYAMA heading, after Yama and Niyama.
- The mark after "Guru" is a footnote that explains Vedanta, not a closing quotation mark. So "Practice alone..." is Jois's own sentence, not a text he is quoting.
- That meets the lineage rule: the source is Jois's own book, in a translation the translators' note says he reviewed.
- The card was right to drop the two famous lines. In this edition, "99% practice" appears only in Sharath's Foreword. I found no printed source for "all is coming".
- About 24 words. Content-safe.

What I fixed:
1. Year. The copyright page says "ORIGINALLY PUBLISHED IN THE KANNADA LANGUAGE IN 1962". Eddie Stern's foreword says Jois began writing it in 1958 and it was first published in 1962. So the "who" year is now 1962, not 1958.
2. Translator. The book's Acknowledgments name "Sri Vishwanath Kadam and Dr. H. L. Chandrashekar, translators". Eddie Stern published the 1999 English edition and wrote a foreword, but the book does not credit him as translator.
3. Publisher dates. North Point Press did not publish in 1999. The copyright page reads: first English edition 1999 by Eddie Stern/Patanjali Yoga Shala, North Point 2002, "this edition, 2010".
4. "Part One". No "Part One" heading appears in the text. The catalog contents read "Yama -- Niyama -- Pranayama -- Surya namaskara and yoga asanas", so I removed it.
5. Meaning line. I added one checkable fact (21 words, no em dash). Eddie Stern's foreword in this same edition says Jois saw Krishnamacharya's demonstration in October-November 1927, asked to learn as "a boy of only twelve", and "practiced with Krishnamacharya every day". It also says "it was quite some time before he understood the method and philosophy". The 1927 and age-twelve lines also turn up in search-inside of the linked scans; the every-day and understanding lines I only read in the full-text copy.

Not confirmed: the printed page number.

Do not share archive.org/details/YogaMala. It is a full ebook copy of the 2010 edition and probably an unauthorized upload. I used it only to read the text.

good.quote: ...having seen it is not as good as understanding it; understanding it is not as good as doing it. ... He who carries it out, knows it thoroughly.
good.work: The Works of Hsuntze, tr. Homer H. Dubs, Probsthain's Oriental Series Vol. XVI, London: Arthur Probsthain, 1928, Book VIII 'The Merit of the Confucian', p. 113
good.meaning: Seeing it and even understanding it are only steps. Doing it is the last step, where you truly know it.
good.reason:
I could not refute this card. The quote is real and word for word, so I only tidied it. I downloaded the archive.org OCR (2015.103953.Works-Of-Hsuntze_djvu.txt). Page 113 has the running header "VIII THE MERIT OF THE CONFUCIAN 113" and reads: "...having seen it is not as good as understanding it; understanding it is not as good as doing it. The development of scholarship is to the extreme of doing it, and that is its end and goal. He who carries it out, knows it thoroughly." The title page confirms "Probsthain's Oriental Series Vol. XVI", Homer H. Dubs, London (41 Great Russell Street), 1928. Book VIII starts on p. 93 under the heading "The Merit of the Confucian". The details page returns 200, and the passage is on scan leaf n115. The DLI record marks the book "Out_of_copyright", and a 1928 publication has been US public domain since 2024. The quote is 27 words.

Two small fixes. (1) Quote: the original has a full stop after "doing it", so the cut should read "doing it. ... He" and not "doing it... He". (2) Meaning: the old line opened with "Hearing", but the quoted text never mentions hearing. Dubs translates that earlier step as "learned", and it falls outside the quote anyway, so I changed the line to match what readers see. "Last step" is fair, since Dubs calls doing "its end and goal". The new line is 20 words, plain English, with no em dash.

Safety: the quoted lines have no rulers, war or politics. The same page talks about rulers employing Confucians and footnotes conquering enemies, but none of that is in the quote. The idea that you only truly know something by doing it fits the theme well.

FLAG: this is the permitted Xunzi exception, because Xunzi was used on 1 Oct. The repo has no record of the 1 Oct line, so I could not confirm it came from a different passage. Check that before posting.

good.who: Wang Yangming · Instructions for Practical Life, 1518
good.quote: The situation may be likened to a man traveling. When (by walking) he has covered a stage, he understands that stage... In this way he gradually reaches his destination.
good.work: The Philosophy of Wang Yang-ming, trans. Frederick Goodrich Henke (Open Court, 1916), Book I, Instructions for Practical Life, Part II, p. 95. Public domain.
good.meaning: A traveller understands each part of the road only by walking it, and step by step he arrives.
good.reason: I tried to refute this card and could not. I downloaded the full text from archive.org (https://archive.org/download/philosophyofwang00wanguoft/philosophyofwang00wanguoft_djvu.txt), and the quote matches it word for word on the page headed "INSTRUCTIONS FOR PRACTICAL LIFE 95". That includes Henke's own bracket "(by walking)" and the spelling "traveling". The ellipsis leaves out exactly one sentence: "When he reaches a fork in the road and is in doubt he makes inquiry, and having made inquiry he again proceeds." It does not change the meaning, and the quote is 29 words. The table of contents puts Part II on pp. 73 to 108, so p. 95 is in Part II, which Lu Ch'eng recorded. The title page says Open Court Publishing Co., London and Chicago, 1916. The archive.org metadata marks it NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT (US). The year 1518 is backed by Henke's own biography (pp. 19 to 20): in the 13th year of Cheng Te (1518), in the eighth month, the disciple Hsieh K'an cut the blocks of the Instructions for Practical Life. Standard scholarship (Wing-tsit Chan) says that first printing held the records of Hsu Ai, Lu Ch'eng and Hsieh K'an, which is Part I of today's text, so this passage was in it. The context fits the theme well: the sentences just before say a man who does not make the effort "will continually talk and yet never comprehend". The meaning line is 18 words, uses simple English and has no em dash. It does not need a year fact, because this is a sage's teaching, not a life story. I also checked the backup line on p. 55 ("Knowledge is the beginning of practice; doing is the completion of knowing."), and it is also word for word. Safety: the quote is only about walking a road. Nothing about Wang's official or military career is mentioned, so keep the caption on his teaching. Wang Yangming is not on this week's used list.

good.quote: However much thou art read in theory, if thou hast no practice thou art ignorant.
good.work: The Gulistan, trans. James Ross, Chapter VIII 'Of the Duties of Society', maxim III. In The Persian Literature, Vol. 2 (Project Gutenberg eBook #13060). Public domain.
good.meaning: Reading a lot about something is not enough. If you never practise it, you still do not really know it.
good.reason: I tried to refute it and could not. I downloaded https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/13060/pg13060.txt. The Gutenberg header says it is by Sadi, translated by James Ross. At lines 4009-4012, under CHAPTER VIII 'Of the Duties of Society', maxim III, the text says: '...he who acquired science and did not practise it:--However much thou art read in theory, if thou hast no practice thou art ignorant.' That matches the card word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation. The quote is 15 words and is a complete sentence, so it needs no ellipsis. The chapter title and maxim number are correct. The two backup lines in the notes are also exact: maxim XLII is at lines 4330-4331 ('Whoever acquires knowledge and does not practise it resembles him who ploughs his land and leaves it unsown.') and maxim LXXXII at line 4571 ('a theorist without practice is a tree without fruit'). The year 1258 is right. Wikipedia's Gulistan article, citing Encyclopaedia Iranica, says it was written in 1258 CE, and Saadi's own introduction dates it to April 1258. The Saadi_Shirazi article also says it was completed in 1258. Saadi is not on the used-this-week list. The words we quote contain no politics, royalty, war or religious conflict. Maxim II nearby mentions a king, and Saadi lived through the 1258 fall of Baghdad, but neither is quoted or mentioned on the card. Nothing mocks a god or sage, and the 'beast of burden' insult is correctly left out. The meaning line is 20 words in plain English with no em dash, and it says the same thing as the quote. A checkable life fact is not needed because this is a 'sage' card, not a 'life' card. I chose not to add his '30 years of travel', because Wikipedia says his life story is uncertain. The quote fits the theme well: practice, not theory, is what gives real knowledge. One small option is to use the plain-text cache URL above as source_url, since it lands right on the exact wording.

good.quote: Although this inconceivable dharma is abundant in each person, it is not actualized without practice, and it is not attained without realization.
good.work: Bendowa (Discourse on the Practice of the Way), 1231. The English is as quoted on page 2 of 'Shusho Itto' by Rev. Seijun Ishii (Komazawa University), translated by Rev. Issho Fujita with Rev. Tonen O'Connor and Rev. Zuiko Redding, in the Basic Key Terms of Soto Zen Teaching series on the official Sotoshu English site.
good.meaning: Dogen trained in China from 1223 to 1227. The good stuff is inside you, but it only shows up when you practise.
good.reason:
I tried to refute the card and could not. I made two small fixes.

1) Quote: I downloaded the official PDF and pulled out its text. Page 2 has the line word for word, punctuation included: "Although this inconceivable dharma is abundant in each person, it is not actualized without practice, and it is not attained without realization." It is 22 words, well under the 30 limit. Just before it, Ishii writes that Dogen added "practice over eight years" to Nangaku's story "to emphasize that it is necessary to have a continuous practice to activate realization." That fits today's theme, that understanding comes from doing.

2) Attribution and year: Bendowa is Dogen's own text, and its date of 1231 is confirmed in two places. Soto Zen's Key Terms PDF no. 2 by Rev. Kodo Takeuchi (sotozen.com/eng/library/key_terms/pdf/key_terms02.pdf) says "In 1231, four years after returning from China... Dogen Zenji wrote Bendowa". Wikipedia's Bendowa page gives 1231 too. The translation credit on the card is right: the PDF ends with "Translated by Rev. Issho Fujita Assisted by Rev. Tonen O'Connor and Rev. Zuiko Redding."

3) Fixes: (a) The rules ask for one checkable fact for a real life, and the old meaning line had none. I added Dogen's years of training in China. The official Soto Zen glossary (sotozen.com/eng/library/glossary/individual.html?key=d_gen) says "In 1223, Dogen accompanied Myozen to China" and he trained in monasteries "before his return to Japan in 1227." The new line is exactly 22 words, in simple English, with no em dash. (b) In the work field, I changed the English title to "Discourse on the Practice of the Way", which is listed on Wikipedia. I could not check the card's title "Talk on Wholehearted Practice of the Way" against an open source. I also named the series by its real title, "Basic Key Terms of Soto Zen Teaching".

4) Rules: Dogen (1200 to 1253) is not on this week's used list; the Buddha/Dhammapada is a different source. This is not a famous misattribution, since it comes straight from the official site of the Soto school, which Dogen founded. Nothing touches politics, royalty, war, disasters or crime, and nothing mocks a religion. It makes no claims about Ashtanga lineage. good.who: Aristotle · Nicomachean Ethics II.1, 4th century BCE
good.quote: For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre...
good.work: Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, Chapter 1 (Bekker 1103a32-34), translated by W. D. Ross, The Works of Aristotle vol. IX (Oxford: Clarendon Press, first edition 1925; public domain in the US). I downloaded the MIT page and the Wikisource proofread scan. Both have this exact text in Book II ch. 1 at 1103a, and Aristotle is not on the used list. Four things needed fixing. (1) DATE OF THE TRANSLATION: the card says "Oxford, 1908", which is wrong. The Wikisource scan of Works of Aristotle vol. IX says "First Edition, 1925", and Ross's preface is dated July 1925. The 1908 date probably comes from Ross's Metaphysics. (2) SPELLING: the printed Ross text reads "lyre-players", with a hyphen. Wikisource has it mid-line, and the 1925 World's Classics scan on archive.org (in.ernet.dli.2015.240820) breaks it as "lyre-/players". So the card's note that Ross writes "lyreplayers" as one word is false. That spelling only comes from how MIT's digital copy handled the hyphen. Even the MIT text-only file uses "lyre-players" a few lines further down. I switched the source URL to Wikisource, which matches the printed page, and kept MIT as a second source. (3) END OF THE QUOTE: in the source, "lyre" is followed by a semicolon and the sentence goes on ("so too we become just by doing just acts..."). The card put a period there, which made it look like the sentence ended. I used an honest ellipsis instead. The cut still stops before the next sentence about legislators and states, so the content rule is met. The quote is 29 words. (4) YEAR: "c. 340 BCE" has no support. Wikipedia says no one agrees on when it was written, and the traditional view (Ross's) puts it in 335-322 BCE, so I changed it to "4th century BCE". About copyright: Ross died in 1971, so the translation is public domain in the US only (Wikisource tag PD/US|1971), not everywhere. The meaning line is fine: 18 words, simple, no em dash, and it says what the quote says.

The 1909 Doubleday copyright covers Piano Questions Answered alone. Both the Gutenberg copyright page and the archive.org records show the combined edition is Theodore Presser, 1920. good.who: Michael Faraday · Letter to Dr. Becker, 1860
good.quote: I was never able to make a fact my own without seeing it... All the work had to be my own.
good.work: Letter to Dr. Becker, 25 October 1860, quoted in Silvanus P. Thompson, Michael Faraday, His Life and Work (1898), p. 244. The full letter is in Bence Jones, The Life and Letters of Faraday, vol. 2 (1870), pp. 439-440.

The quote and its year check out, but the card needed two small fixes.

Quote: I downloaded Gutenberg #65735 (Thompson, Michael Faraday, His Life and Work, 1898; the title page says 1898). (2) The meaning line said the experiments cost "a few pence". The source says "a few pence per week", so I changed it to "simple chemistry experiments that cost a few pence a week". It is 19 words with no long dash.

Safety: Bence Jones calls Dr. Becker "Prince Albert's secretary". The card says nothing about that, nor about Faraday's religious sect, and it should stay that way because of the royalty rule. Faraday is not on this week's used list. The quote is 20 words.
